interviewQuestions.question: Implicit vs explicit feedback — which is more common in practice, and why?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by defining both: explicit feedback is a deliberate signal (a star rating, a thumbs up); implicit is inferred from behavior (clicks, watch-time, dwell time). In practice, implicit dominates — the vast majority of users never rate anything, but almost everyone clicks, scrolls, or watches. Netflix, YouTube, and Amazon are all trained primarily on implicit signals because that's the only data that exists at the volume needed to train a model well.

The trade-off is honesty of signal: a rating tells you the user liked something; a click just tells you they were curious enough to try it, which is a much noisier proxy for genuine preference — someone can click and then immediately bounce. So most systems treat implicit feedback as the primary training signal but calibrate it carefully (e.g. weighting by watch-time, not just play count) to reduce that noise.

**Testing:** whether you understand that real-world recommenders are built on noisy, abundant implicit signal rather than clean, scarce explicit signal — and that this shapes model and loss-function choices downstream.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Implicit vs explicit feedback

interviewQuestions.question: Someone claims your platform has 'solved cold start' because you have hundreds of millions of user interactions overall. Why is that claim wrong?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The claim conflates two completely different quantities: how much data exists across the whole platform, and how much data exists for the *specific* user or item currently being scored. Collaborative filtering — the technique that benefits most from platform-wide data volume — works by finding patterns across many users' interactions, and its ability to make a good prediction for any one user depends on having interaction history *for that user*, not on how much data exists for everyone else combined. A brand-new user with zero clicks has exactly the same amount of usable signal on a platform with a billion total interactions as they would on a platform with a thousand — the billion interactions belong to other users, and none of them substitute for this specific user's missing history.

This is easy to miss because "more data helps" is true in almost every other ML context — more training examples generally improve a model's ability to generalize. But cold start isn't a generalization problem in that sense; it's a missing-input problem for a specific entity. No amount of data about other users or other items changes the fact that this particular new user or new item has an untrained ID embedding with nothing meaningful learned into it — the model has nothing to key off of *for that specific ID*, regardless of the platform's overall scale.

What actually addresses cold start is architectural, not volume-based: onboarding flows that elicit a few explicit preferences upfront, popularity or trending fallbacks for brand-new users, and content-based signals (item features that exist independent of any interaction history) to surface new items before they've accumulated engagement. A platform's overall data volume is irrelevant to any of these fixes — a small platform with good onboarding can handle cold start better than a massive platform with none.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate why aggregate data volume and per-entity data availability are different axes, rather than just asserting cold start persists as an unexplained fact.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why platform scale doesn't solve cold start

interviewQuestions.question: You're designing the training label for a video platform's recommender using implicit feedback. Why is 'did the user click play' a worse label than 'did the user watch most of the video,' and how would you construct a better one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A click/play event only tells you the user was curious enough to try something — it's a very early, low-commitment signal that can be triggered by a misleading thumbnail or title just as easily as by genuine interest, and it says nothing about whether the content actually delivered value once they started watching. Someone can click a video and abandon it ten seconds in because the thumbnail oversold what was actually inside — training a model to maximize that signal specifically rewards exactly this pattern, since the model has no way to distinguish a genuinely satisfying click from a bait-and-abandon one; both look identical as a raw "played" event.

Watch-time completion is a meaningfully better proxy because it requires the user to keep engaging *after* the initial click, which filters out a large share of the bait-and-abandon cases — a video watched to 90% completion is much stronger evidence of genuine value delivered than one abandoned at 5%. It's not a perfect label either: a long video watched to 90% and a short video watched to 90% represent very different absolute engagement, so raw completion percentage alone can still mislead across content of different lengths, and some content is designed to be sampled briefly and still be valuable (a quick reference clip).

A more robust construction I'd reach for: combine multiple signals into the label rather than relying on any single one — weight by absolute watch duration alongside completion percentage, incorporate explicit downstream signals like whether the user returned to watch more from the same creator, and where available, occasional survey-based "was this worth your time" signals as a periodic calibration check against the proxy the model actually trains on. The general principle: push the label as far downstream from the raw click as the available data allows, since every step downstream filters out more noise from content that was clicked but not actually valuable.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the specific failure mode of a shallow proxy (rewards curiosity-bait, not genuine value) and propose a concrete, layered improvement rather than just naming "watch-time" as a fix.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Constructing a better implicit-feedback training label
